blocks.x: And if there's some books that I can...
Speaking of right names, what's yours?

My right name that was given to me by my father and mother, first name, Godfrey, G-O-D-F-R-E-Y, the second name, Mayer, M-A-Y-O-R, the third name, Hirsch, capital H-I-R-S-C-H. The reason my middle name is Mayer and not Major is because when my grandfather, Mayor, Major came to this country, there was always a screw-up with the... What do you call that up there when they're coming in? Immigration? Yeah, from a foreign... Immigration. They pronounce the word Mayer, Major, like in Spanish, it's Mayor. Mayor. So they put the M-A-Y-O-R. So I do have some relatives by the name of Major, but I got the name of Mayor. Mayor. And my mother told Shep Morrison once, she says, you may be a mayor for four terms, but my son will always be a mayor. Mayor. What's your name? My name is Curtis Gerdy. Okay.
And I'm Dick Allen, and we're all picking up, and we're on the first reel. What's today's date?
Today is the 16th, I think. No, 20th. 20th? Yeah.
20th of October.
October 20th, 1987.
Oh, I forgot to ask you where you were born.
I was born in Greenville, Mississippi, the Queen City of the Delta, Washington County, Mississippi.
How did that happen?
My father,
pardon me,

my father was a band, an orchestra leader. He was the orchestra leader at the Grand Opera House, which was a theater in Greenville, and he was the orchestra leader. And they used to have all kind of shows coming through there in those days. It was not an opera. Exactly as an opera, like La Tosca, or the great operas. It was, they had attractions of vaudeville, shows, road shows, and also minstrel shows, and things like that. What they used to refer to as burlesque opera, huh? Yeah. Yeah.
And Charles Hirsch, where was he from?

Charles Hirsch was my grandfather. He was from Alsace-Lorraine. Now, one week, Alsace-Lorraine is Germany, and one next week, it's France. I never have been able to find out exactly where my grandfather, what city he was born from there. My cousin told me someplace where he was born, but I never did find out. I mean, I never knew.
Where did he come to in this country?

He came to, originally, he went to Baton Rouge, and then he came to New Orleans. And, he, he came here about 1870, around that time. I have his marriage license over here, and his citizenship papers. Yeah. They were in the wall, hanging on the wall over there. That, that was my grandfather's, let's see.
I'll turn it off. It's rolling. Okay.

State of Louisiana, City of New Orleans. No men be by these presents. Charles Hirsch. Oh, this is their marriage certificate. This is their marriage certificate. It's vain, I don't know, 14th day, of 1864, they were married. They were married. This is their, this is their marriage certificate. This is, they were married here?
Yeah.

In 1864? Yeah. And this is, my grandfather's, this is his, naturalization papers. And, I don't know what it says here. I don't see the date. Oh, yeah. Yeah. On this, sitting in the lawns, on this, 13th day of October, in the year of, our Lord, 1868. 1868.
Mm-hmm.
was when he became a citizen. So, he actually, became, came over to this country, probably about 1867.
So, it was right about that same time, then?

He had a brother, by the name of Lazar Hirsch, who, ended up in, in Amal, Louisiana. And they had, he had a grocery store, a general merchandise store, and later, they were the post office, in Amal, Louisiana. And his daughter, Julia Hirsch, was, later, made postmistress, after, after Lazar Hirsch died. And he had another, he had a son, Henry Hirsch, who went over to, Narco, that's right above, St. Rose. Of course, I mean, I don't know, what these towns are called now, Amal, and St. Rose, if they still, call that, and what not. But they, they did very well, and they prospered well. And, not millionaires, but, they were pretty well off it.
What about, Charles Hirsch's business? Did he rent instruments, to musicians?

No, he didn't rent instruments, no, Charles Hirsch was not a musician. Charles Hirsch came here, and from my knowledge, or what was told to me, he came here, and he went into, the bric-a-brac business. In other words, fancy ornaments, and so forth, and so on. And at one time, he, we at one time, had one of the finest stores, in the city of New Orleans. Of course, being down there, on Frenchman and Decatur Street, which he bought, that building in 18, around 1870, or maybe before that, the date's up there, on that, on that deed, he, he had, what, the fancy, fancy, fancy, It was a gift shop. You see? A gift shop.

Read that. It says, from Hirsch, with an S on it, Hirsch's gift shop. China glassware toys and general house furnishing goods. 501 to 511 Frenchman, corner Decatur Street, phone Hemlock 775. And so they had a plate, a calendar plate from 1911. Decatur and Frenchman, it says on it, yeah.

They used to give these things away. Very pretty, uh, lady. It's not good china. It's not good china. It's what we call the china mud. That's mud china. But, uh, I'll show you the difference between. Now, that's one, and this is another one from another year. That's my, this friend of ours, who were friends of ours, gave us, gave us these plates. And, uh, the only difference between mud china and good china. You can hear this.
Right. It rings.
Yeah. Oh, it's the same way with glassware. Mm-hmm.
Uh-huh.

Uh, here's one that we have 11 of them. We have 11 of them. That's all we got left. This is what people call Irish crystal. I know that's Irish crystal. We've had it. I don't know how long. But, uh, look through that. It's like looking through. Mm-hmm. It's like looking through a lens. Yeah.
Wow. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
It's like a bell, huh? A bell.
That's Irish crystal. I have an Irish crystal bill, but I'm afraid to do it. Do that.
You don't become afraid to do it if you know how to do it. Yeah.
Wow.

And we've got different things in here, like these things that came from the store. So, this is what we, uh, this is, then we went into the rental end of it. We went into the rental end. This, this was the China where, that we used to rent. Really? That's Austrian China. That's what you call eggshell. I've heard a chance to see it.
Yeah. Ooh.
Two handles. That's a bouillon color. Beautiful. Wonderful.
Wonderful. It's a soup.
It's a soup. Yeah. But, uh, this was what we used to rent. And we used to rent. It's our story of glassware. But, uh, we finally, and then he finally started going into the rental business.
Mm-hmm.

Rental business. Well, rental. Rental business was created in the later years. In other words, we created a slogan called it, Entertainments Furnished. And people would ring us up and say, Entertainments Furnished. And we'd say, what kind of entertainment can you furnish us with? Yeah. So that's when it got away from Entertainments Furnished to Rent. Rent all. Rent all. Rental. Rental. R-E-N-T-A-L. And then rent all. And there's all the, there's all the, uh, dies from the, uh, stationery that we used to have. Mm-hmm. Printed. That's a picture of the truck up there.
Yeah.

And that was on the telephone book. And that was some of my father's stationery, the two things there. And those are things that we had. Since then they don't use that type of, uh, uh, printing anymore. They don't use the, uh, it's all, it's all now.
Is that what you call a cut?
It's a cut. Yeah. Those are cuts, different cuts. Yeah. They don't use that anymore. Yeah. Very seldom they use it. They can use it, but I don't think they got the machines for them anymore.
Well, everything is so different. I don't know how they get computers.
Computerized. Yeah.
Did you live around Decatur and, uh, Frenchman ever?

No. I used to stay down there with them. I loved it down there because I was, my uncle, who I was very attached to, married to my aunt, my father's sister. And, uh, I loved it down there. I enjoyed it. My uncle was a, was a cabinet maker. And, uh, that's where I think I got my knowledge of cabinet making. And he was quite a guy. And, uh, I liked him very much. In fact, I used to, I lived up on Napoleon Avenue and Franklin, which is Napoleon Avenue, and Liberty now. Mm-hmm. Right. Not Liberty. I mean, uh, Warnsley. Warnsley, right. And, uh, I used to get on a streetcar, about a half a block from my house, for a nickel, and I'd be down at the store without transferring. Used to go, the Cronolet streetcar used to go, Cronolet, Napoleon Avenue, Cronolet, Cronolet, across Bourbon Street. Down Bourbon to Esplanade, across Esplanade to Decatur by the firehouse, and then down around that section, down Decatur Street. And went down Decatur Street. I don't know how, I don't remember how far it did, but I managed to get off the Frenchman in Decatur.
Did any of your, uh, uncles play music?
No. I had one uncle who was an actor.
Mm-hmm.
He was a, a thespian. I gotta get it right. A thespian. He was, uh, he was quite a guy.
But your dad was the only one that played, huh?

My, uh, father was the only one that played. He played the Cronolet, and, uh, he played pretty, pretty good. In fact, Johnny Detroit had a great respect for him, a great admiration for him, and he played for him. I mean, uh, great admiration for him. Yeah. Uh, when Johnny went to New York, he was working on the fountain grill of the Rosefeld Hotel, and he asked my daddy to substitute for him playing his place, and he did for about six weeks, I think it was. And he was very elated the way my father played. He said, my daddy could play a ballad better than anybody I ever heard. He had a beautiful tone on the clarinet, on the cornet, and he played the cornet. It wasn't until later that he played, uh, that he went to trumpet. Yeah.
Well, where was this that he substituted for?

The fountain lounge. The fountain lounge. The fountain lounge. The fountain lounge. The fountain lounge. The fountain lounge. Well, it was later the fountain lounge of the Rosefeld Hotel. Forest Grill. Bailey's is there now.
Uh-huh, okay.

You know where Bailey's is? On Brown Street. All right. At one time, the Rosefeld Hotel used to be right, right where it is, except that where they had the, in later years, became the fountain, fountain lounge, and the breakfast room for the, breakfast room or the fountain lounge was where Bailey's is now. In other words, they used to do, when Kellner was there, they used to, on weekends when they'd have a big crowd, he was playing in the fountain, in the fountain room, fountain room lounge, and uh, they would open up the other room down there for the overflow of the people. And there was a dance floor, uh, that was, uh, like a dance floor down there. I think it was a hardwood floor down there that they'd let them use as a dance floor. They would dance and then have the sound that was coming down there and they could dance down there. They'd be dancing down there, dancing up in the fountain lounge.
Did you play with Kellner, Dan?

I said, I was, I was sort of, I was sort of Leon's godfather. Really? Whenever he needed a substitute, when he went to New York, I'd end up playing piano for him. And, uh, whenever he wanted to fire somebody, he'd have to ask me, how do you fire him? And we were very close. In fact, the last thing he asked me to do is how to, how to get out of, of, uh, get out of, uh, a losing proposition belonging to the New York local. And I told him I've got the same problem that we've been in so long that we pay for our life insurance. And if we get out now, we're going to lose it if we don't continue to pay for it. It's just like being a member of our local down here. That if you know, if you're, if you're, if you're a, if you're a honorary member that you were up until this last year, where you, you now have to pay dues. Mm-hmm. If you've already paid up your dues and paid your thousand dollars, if you, if you, if you de-met, well, you're out a thousand dollars in the event you're dying. You're, you're getting older all the time. There was a better chance for your family to get a thousand dollars. So I figured it out mathematically for Leon that if he paid his dues for the next twenty-four years and, and, and died, his, his state would get four hundred dollars.
But he had to die within so many years. But, uh, maybe he'd get a few projects or something.
You know, he's down in Florida now, you know. Yeah. I've heard that but I don't know where he is. I know where he is.
Is he still working at the Broadwater?
No. No. He's not at the Broadwater anymore. That's Mrs. Brown. That's sorts of Biloxi. No, he's down in Boca Raton, Florida, I think. Some friends of mine told me they saw him down there.
But is he, is he.

Yeah. There's no chicken anymore. Is he playing down there? Yeah. He's playing. He's a damn good piano player. Yeah. But he's quite a guy. We've always had good relations between us. In fact he wanted me to come over to Biloxi. He wanted to go up to New York for something, I don't remember who it was, and he offered me a job over in Biloxi. It was a very beneficent job, fifty dollars a night, and room and board. But I didn't think I could afford to, I think I eat more than fifty dollars a day. I told him I had other contracts that I had to fulfill and I didn't want to hurt his feelings. But he tried to get a piano player to get over there. I mean he's getting at least three or four hundred dollars a week, and he wanted to get rid of it for nothing. I don't need publicity anymore.
Not that kind of publicity, huh?

His son was playing drums with him. He's a good drummer, and they had a bass player over there. I don't know his name, but he's a member of our union. But he is one hell of a good bass player. I mean electric bass. He's got a beautiful ear. I made a record with him. I made a record with him. And this boy, he reminded me that he was Leon's piano player, a bass player. But he is one hell of a classy, faking bass player that plays another netto. But he plays electric. Doesn't play upright, huh?
No.
I never heard him play upright. He was playing electric. It might have been Tim Jackson. I don't know but he was good. He was here in town. But he plays upright.
He plays both. Very good.
I'll tell you this was the thing about Netto. If Netto knew what Keya was in, he didn't make a mistake. And I mean even if the tune would digress from say a C to an A flat to an E major or from
whatever, he could hear it.
He knew it. And a lot of these bass players, you're an exception. You didn't get my compliments.
Well thank you.

But a lot of these bass players, when they start playing flat at 13ths and flat at 14ths and flat at 18ths, they don't know what the fuck they're doing. They're just hitting them on. I mean Tony Lausa is another one of those great. He can sing the Bachemagula or something like that but he can't play all the things you are. Is that right? No kidding. No. No bass. Jack Abel let him go. And Jack's got a pretty keen ear.
Yeah.

In fact I had Jack play out at the Norris Country Club. And he had a job earlier and I told him, I said don't worry, I'll play for a half hour until you get there. And I got out there for a half hour and believe me, he wasn't getting the same notes as I was. And I think I know what the notes are. Yeah. Yeah. But this boy was good and Leon's a well-school pianist. He's 90% bullshit but he's a good boy.
So how did you get started playing? Me?

That's a long story. I was a child prodigy on the piano. I started, my sister was taking piano lessons. My mother, let me say this, my mother was a very fine pianist and a violinist. And my father was a very good trumpet player, a good cornet player. And there was always music in our house. And I used to like to play the snare drum. I like drums. And my daddy didn't want me to play drums. The only thing good about a drummer is that you're the first one on the job and the last one to leave and you better have a truck.
He's right.

It's getting worse today. That's right. It's getting worse today. You'll see Ray Franson go on a job. I used to tell Ray, all I need is a bass drum and a snare drum. Oh, I have to bring the other equipment with me. And he sets up like this. So I have a snare drum bought from Grunewalds, Mr. Eckert. Old man Eckert. I think he sold every musician in town his first instrument. And my daddy bought me a snare drum. And he wouldn't buy me a set of drums. So my sister was studying piano. And I started looking at her books. And I'm reading her books and I'm reading before she's out of book one, I'm in book three. So the teacher heard me playing one day when she came to teach my sister. And she told my mother, she says, as long as I'm here, she says, I could teach your son too. She was paying 50 cents a lesson for my sister. And she says, I'm going to charge you two bits of lessons from Godfrey. I got a grand lesson for two bits. And I did very well. I played before Philip Gordon, who was a, after I started playing pretty good, I played before him. And he was a guy that used to make the roles for the Aeolian piano. The grand one. They started with the Aeolian roles for the grand pianos. In fact, he gave a concert and I was at the concert. And he was giving a demonstration to how you could, it was so realistic that you wouldn't know if it was a role or the artist playing on the thing. And after the concert, we were talking and talking and I said, well, I'll never be a good piano player. And I said, because my hands are so small. He said, let me see your hands. He said, look at mine. These are not much larger than yours. So that doesn't make any difference, small hands or large hands. It helps a little, but it doesn't hurt. So then Ida Flatricu, who was a teacher at Newcomb College, took me as a special student. I used to go up there on Saturdays. My father couldn't afford to pay for it. My grandmother, the mayor, she paid for it. She used to send my mother $5 a week for me. She charged me $5 a lesson, which was very, very expensive in those days. And I studied with Ida for quite a while until I lived across the street from a park and they were playing baseball and football. And here I am playing . So I wanted to play ball and then I wanted to play drums. And my uncle was in town and he bought me a bass drum and a couple of the things that go on it. And I went with Vic, did you know, do you remember Vic Pellegrini? Did you ever hear of Vic Pellegrini? I've heard the name. Vic Pellegrini, I don't remember his father's name but I think his father's name was Vic Pellegrini too.
Did he play trumpet, Vic, the young one?
No, the young Vic Pellegrini was a piano player. Okay. He goes by the name now of Victor Pell. Victor Pell. He was, in later years he became Blossom Seely's accompanist. Ah, okay.
Uh-huh.

Yeah, I know that. Later years she became a partner. And he was down here, I worked with them, we used to play in a dance hall down on Elysium Fields. You have to go out on the gallery and play a warm up tune to get the customers to come in. And I don't remember who the hell was playing the piano but I know Vic was playing piano. I don't think we had a bass fiddle. We had a trombone and his father played the carnet. I don't remember who played trombone but these were all adults. And Vic and I, we were still in Warren Easton High School. We were still in high school and this was before 1926 when I graduated from Warren Easton. And I played with them for quite a few years. And then Vic went away and he went to New York. He went on the stage. He was down here, oh maybe ten years or so ago. And oddly enough, I was talking to him about when we were up in, he was in the food process, the food business. He was, we were up in, out of Baltimore, eastern Maryland. And when we were up there for a wedding, his friend of mine, we went to a restaurant, I wanted to eat clams, and we went to a restaurant that was like on a bay up there. And it was an old restaurant from the Civil War, from the Revolutionary War and all of that stuff. And we had lunch in there. And oddly enough, I told Vic that when he came down here on a visit and he called me, and I took him all around. Then later, he was, had charge of a big, well you could call them condominiums now, in Washington, D.C. or somewhere maybe in Virginia. That he was in charge of all of this and he had to build kitchens and this and that and the next thing. And it was a big deal. So I took him to the Rivergate and I showed him the kitchens down there and I showed him the kitchens of the Roosevelt Hotel when they were just adding on to the Imperial Ballroom. And we got, we had him out here a couple of times for dinner and renewed our acquaintanceship. And I told him about eastern Maryland, up in Maryland. He said, you know, it's a funny thing, I used to own that place. I sold it. There was some guy that was the, one of the benefits or the donors of the benefactors, and donors of the American Revolution. His name was Morris. The guy, his name was Morris. He was one of the benefactors of the American Revolution. He raised the money. He used to own that place. And I haven't, I haven't heard from Dick in quite a while. But I don't think he's on stage anymore because I mean, I don't think Barterfield's on stage anymore.
To get back to Lesion Fields, I know it's a little bit on the way. Do you remember the corner about that dance hall?
Or the name of the dance hall?
It was probably Burgundy Street. It wasn't where Pete was. Pete was on Royal. He was at Lusitannis, huh? He was on Royal Street.
Yeah, that's the old Lusitannis, isn't it? I don't know.
I can't remember. Pete completely renovated the whole thing. Yeah. He renovated the whole thing.
And, uh, do you remember the name of that dance hall on the Lesion Fields?

No, there was a lot of them down there, around there. They were all upstairs. There was a big open floor on the second floor. And they used to have like a balcony outside. And you'd go outside and you'd play on the balcony and people would know that you were there. And they could hear you and a little lady, 50 cents or something like that, to come over there and dance for a half a buck or a buck all night. Uh-huh. And, uh, no, I don't remember just where it was. It was not where Pete was, but because Pete didn't have a gallery on his place. But it was one of the places, it was a corner place, and it had a gallery. And, uh, we were talking about Lesion Fields.
Which Pete are we talking about when you say Pete? Pete Fonten. Pete Fonten, okay.
Uh, we were talking about Lesion Fields. Here's something I have. From my grandfather's. I'm gonna have to get around here. Come around.
Okay. Let me get on board. Let me get on board.
Okay. Let me get on board. This is the original surveyor's drawing of our property on Frenchmen and Decatur Street. Uh-huh. This is the guy's name.
George D'Armas.

George D'Armas. Surveyor, Civil Engineer, and Civil Engineer. Now that's before the... 17, 27, and 3 1 1 1st, Cloranelet Street. Now here's the U.S. Mint. Uh-huh. Engine house. They didn't call it the fire station. This is where... This is where Rouge Halls used to be over here. But here's something that'll measure. This is Decatur Street. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Formerly Victory Road. Mm-hmm. This is... This is Charter Street. Mm-hmm. This is Charter Street. Formerly Moro. Yeah. Did you know that? Well, I had read about all this stuff a long time ago. I'd forgotten it all. This is... This is... This is... This is... This is... This is... This is... This is Esplanade. This is Esplanade. This is over here.
Yeah, right. Got the tracks for Sugar Mary.
Um... Smokey Mary. Yes, sir. Pontchartrain and Lake Railroad. That's what... That's what it was. The railroad and depot.
This is Esplanade.

That's when I had it over here. Yeah, right. Got the tracks for Sugar Mary... Smokey Mary. Yes, sir. Pontchartrain and Lake Railroad. That's what... That's what it was. Mm-hmm. The railroad and depot. This is Esplanade Street. Not heavy. Then this is Louisville and Nashville Railroad. This is Esplanade Street. The tracks used to come around here and go up to the LNN station.
Mm-hmm. And that's before they changed the number, so it's... Yeah. Got to be way back.

Now this... Well, they changed the street numbers. This was done April the 29th, April the 23rd, 1890. That's when my grandfather bought this building. But he came here by 1870. The Jew for the fees, 275 feet at 2 cents a foot, $5.50.
Look at this. Jeez.
This is his envelope. This is the envelope where it came in. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Say it again, Moise? Moise, M-O-I-S-E.
And the last name Hirsch. Hirsch, yeah. Okay. This is the second reel of Godfrey Hirsch, and it's the 20th of October...
October, 1987.
And where are we? What's the address here?
5921 Marshall Foch, New Orleans, Louisiana, 70124, 504, area code, 4863930. Thank you. This is my uncle here. Now this is a story. I have to tell you this story.
Okay.

My niece, my cousin, whose father owned a big department store that hired a lot of Christian girls, and us being Jewish, she took this picture down to the store and asked these people, do you know who this is? And being a nice Christian girl, she says, oh yes, that's Christ our Lord and Savior. She says, no it's not, that's my uncle. He was in Chardamon with the Lambs Club, and every year they used to put on the Lambs Gamble, and they did have one around Christmas time that they put on, and he was portrayed the part of Christ. He not only portrayed that part, he portrayed the part of MacArthur. When they had a bond sale or something. Huh. This is him. He died, he was 86 when he died. He was quite a guy. He was quite something, he was in a show that he was in there called Lightman. He was a British officer. And these were the things that he did as a sideline, as a professional model. He did that. This is him there for SL. And that's your uncle.
Yeah.

There's one over here. That was for Ethel gas. This is for Ethel gas again. This is something else. Here's Cherville 1934. It was on this boat. Supposedly on a boat. This was a big app for Chesapeake Church. Chesterfield cigarettes and this for Chesterfield. There you go, different ads that he did. He did a lot of ads. He was a charter member of the Lambs Club. Now this guy, he's on a program as a world trans. And he looks very much like my uncle. You see the resemblance? Yeah. And I sent him a picture of my uncle and he sent me this back picture of him and he autographed it. What's his name? Can you remember? Henderson something, I can't think of it.
Looks like a Roth or something. Henderson something.
He's in and out of the show now. Yeah. This is my uncle again.
And an ad for Canada to draw. He was gonna do a Scotch ad or something. In Highland Garb.

This is, well this was about, it was in the paper. Scoop around and I had to clear it up. So I cleared it up. And this was, I don't know this. Oh this is the letters. He was a very, he was a very good friend of President Horsfeld. Oh. Oh yeah, more damn pictures taken. Now my niece, my cousin, she made a complete biography of him. Oh.
Yeah. Yeah. You wanted the whole one? No I'll get it.

I'll get it. I'll get it. This is a complete biography of my uncle and his coming to New Orleans play where he played and who he played with and so forth and so on. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm.
Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm.

Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. Mmhm. That's your uncle also? Yeah, he was, you see, he lived at the Lambs Club. Mm-hmm. 130 West 44th Street. The same person as Moyes Hirsch? Yeah. Oh, change his name. Just change his name. And this is one of my other uncles. No. That's Mendelov. I saved this up. This is quite a, I've read a book on Louie. Do you remember him when he was here? Louie? Yeah. I've got a picture of Louie Armstrong sitting, standing in front of Suburban Gardens. Mm-hmm. I don't think you ever heard of Suburban Gardens. Oh, yes. We know a lot of Suburban Gardens. Well, I got a picture of him standing there with his trumpet plate like this. Uh-huh. He followed us in when we left. I knew Louie, and then I knew Louie. That was in 31, you're talking about? Yeah. I don't know what year it was. Probably, maybe. Because that's when Louie came back here and did his stand-up to the Reproduction. Yeah, I think they've got that in the books about Louie. Before that. Yeah, but he came into Suburban Gardens. You don't get the lavalier. Hmm?
You don't get the lavalier microphone. Yeah. I'm going to go get this here now.
You don't get the lavalier microphone.
Yeah.
I'm going to go get this here now. Yeah. I'm going to go get this here now. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
I'm going to go get this here now. Yeah. Yeah.

When they closed.
Here's the blue room there, with Gordon Kirst playing, leading. This is a... Oh, wow. Oh, wow. Louie Macenthal was playing bass. Uh-huh. We had Duke Ellington uniforms, almost.

So you played in this band. Yeah, this is me. All right. All right. Come around here. Did you stay in the blue room after this band? No. After that, we went to the fountain lounge. Oh, okay. Again, it's a name I've heard people say.

Johnny Ronica. Where's Johnny? There he is. Yeah. And Frank Federico. Fitchin'. Don't want my mama. Polké Carrier.

So you say Lou Forbes had the band in there until it closed then, huh? When did it close? What year?

Well, when did I say when did it open? You said in 31. Well, it closed about in 30, 30, closed the end of 31. Uh-huh, okay. This is some of the band, yeah. When did it reopen again? The next day. The next day, okay. They changed his name to the Blue Hawaiian Room.
Ah.

This is Forbes' band. This is Forbes here. I'm going to play the Gentle Motor Show at the other time. Here's Forbes. Red Bowman. Menatana. He's dead. Chory Horton is dead. Mm-hmm. Chester Wicker was a piano player?
Yeah, Chester was a piano.

I never did know him. This is when Gordon had the orchestra.
This is in the Blue Room.

This is the funniest story ever. See this? Uh-huh. We played that, I noticed the other day somehow that was the anniversary of F.R.'s birthday, it was the anniversary of F.R.'s birthday, it was the year that he first started with the March of Dimes. Uh-huh. It was the first time. So we had a big concert down at the Municipal Auditorium. This is the Municipal Auditorium, the stage, the bandstand and everything up here, and they had an American flag up there and Roosevelt's picture on it. And when we got finished, it was not there except until after the finale. Now the band is facing this way, and you can't tell what the hell's in vacuum.
Uh-huh.

So the people applauded, and just about when they stopped applauding, they started applauding again. So Lou Forbes comes out, and he's taking a bow, and he's telling you guys, come on outside and take a bow. We stand about a footwork, taking a bow. But they don't know that they're not clapping for us, they're clapping for Roosevelt's picture, the American flag, that's in back of us. This is a funny story. This is from 1933. And you worked with who at the Sanger? I worked with Forbes. Forbes?
Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. Nine months or so. This is Louie Primer. Uh-huh. Yeah. Ed Fontana, Charlie Hartman. All these guys are dead.

Ed Fontana, any relation to Carl Fontana? No. No. No, no, no. Hector Fontana is his son. Ah, okay. Now, Leo Forbstein. That was his brother. His brother. Was he ever involved down here? No. Did he ever come here? No, no.

He was on the First National. He was at First National. But every one of these people, this is the only guy that I know if he's still alive. Every one of these guys are dead. So Alessandro, this guy dead. This guy dead. This guy dead. Paquet, the clarinet, there's Alessandro, there's Tony Papalia, Charlie Hartman, Fontana, Rico Condona, Johnny Detroit just died, Mike Apparello I know has been dead for quite a while, and Louis Primer's dead. Who goddamn band is dead? That's it that Blair sung Evolution of Music? That was Evolution of Music. 4-28-32. Gosh.
Well, that's a while back.
Yeah. This is when Benny Barrows' band was down here.
They were on the stage, Benny Barrows. Wow. And this is when we were in the pit.

I didn't even know how to spell Marrow. M-E-R-R-O-F-F. Did you work any of the theaters with any other bands besides Marrow? No. I didn't know how to spell Marrow. I didn't know how to spell Marrow. M-E-R-R-O-F-F.

Did you work any of the theaters with any other bands besides Forbes? Yeah, I worked at the, for Minsky, Harold Minsky, when they had a stage show. It's torn down there. The International, Intercontinental. Intercontinental Hotel there. This is Ben Amaroff. I'm looking for that picture. Here's Gus Onry. You probably heard of him. And there's this.

I thought that picture would be in here. This is when we went, Harry Burke and I went to the World's Fair in 33. This is Notre Dame University and this is, these are pictures taken along the road. Who was Harry Burke? Harry Burke was a piano player and an accordion player. More or less a teacher than he was a musician. This is for digging instruments, digging vibes and all. This is me. Really? Yeah, you don't recognize it.
Well you do look a little bit.
I had a mustache there.

Did you play over on the Gulf Coast much in the early years? Oh yeah. You did? Spot jobs. Spot jobs. Who did you play over there mostly with? Pinky and Pete and Al Herrick. In the early years in the 30s. No. It's when we were kids when we got, we got a job over there at the hotels. So in the 20s.
In the 20s. In the 30s. We got a job over at the hotels. And Pete and Al Herg.
In the early years, in the 30s?

Well, not in the 30s. Oh, in the 30s. No, it's when we were kids when we got used to, we'd get a job over there at the hotels. In the 30s, we'd get a job over at the hotels. And you'd play the hotels for lunch and dinner, and you got $17.50 a week, plus food. And you'd work a nightclub, and we lived at the nightclub, and got crabs. Not the kind you eat. Not the kind you eat. And I think we used to get $25 a week for that. So, I mean, they used to give us a little night meal out there, and we slept there, and we played the hotel. That lasted about two weeks, I guess, at the most. I never will forget, there was two guys who were comedians and singers. They used to be songwriters. They were around New Orleans a long time. I forget their names. But they were also waiters. And in those days, the Gulf Coast was very, very cheap. Very cheap. I mean, you'd feel that you paid $5 for a dinner in Chicago. They'd charge you a dollar for a dinner down here. So these guys, they went in business for themselves, and they had a whole set of new checks made. And every time somebody gets for a check for their meal, they didn't get a check that came from the kitchen. They got their checks that they made out themselves. Raised every check, about $8, $10, and they were in business for themselves. So they paid a check for the kitchen for about $2, and they got $8 for the check. So they were six bucks a head. But these guys, I mean, they were really manipulators. And then I'll never forget one night, they didn't get the, they weren't getting paid their money. So they took the, after the place closed, they went and got a hammer and broke the glass on the jackpot on the slot machine and took the quarters out of that. Oh, they were dangerous.
Did Stranicos ever go over to the Gulf Coast? He was from the Gulf Coast.

Ellis was from the Gulf Coast. Yeah. It was Stranicos' man that we used to play over there with Charlie Wagner, Johnny Roniger, Meyer Weinberg, Doc Benitez. You know, he died recently. Oh, yes, he did, yeah. Doc died. Three bass players that worked with me the past 10 years. All died in a very short period of time.
Yes, sir. Who was the ottoman?
Ray Benitez, Frank Netto, and Pat Easterling. Pat was with the, at the, at the Jefferson Orleans with Pat Barbrot.
Yeah, I just didn't know you worked with him.

Yeah, he was with, Pat was with me for ages. In fact, I got, I got, I made Henry Newfield a leader at the Court of the Two Sisters. Joe Fine is a very dear friend of mine. I've known Joe all my life almost. And I was his music advisor down at the, at the, at the Court of the Two Sisters. Uh-huh. And, uh, he needed a band. So I asked Henry if he wanted to work on it. And he got, he got that little, the barber, the piano player. And, uh, he had Pat on bass. He was, I don't remember who played trumpet with him. But, uh, they started playing down there at the Court of the Two Sisters. And they built up quite a, quite a, quite a business.
What did you call him, uh, that plays piano? From across the river? Valentino, Valentino.
Oh, okay. Valentino.
Oh, okay.
Valentino. You know him, uh, Valentino's his name. And, uh, he was down there with them. And, uh, after about three years, they were doing terrific business. Joe comes up and fires him.
Hmm.

And Henry asked him, he said, what'd you fire me for? He said, we don't need you no more. We're doing business. We don't need a man anymore. Uh-huh. So, they, then he let him go. And, uh, Joe never would have told me that, but, uh, Henry did tell me that, because I was, I worked with Henry after, after I left Pete. And I was with Henry with, who was booking most of the Lou Wopps jobs. And, uh, in fact, we had quite a, with Rene, he didn't want, he didn't want Henry to use me. He said, because Henry, Godfrey's a leader. He says, he'll take the jobs. He, he says, he don't need your jobs. He says, uh, he'll pay you a commission on the jobs that he gets if, if it, if it interferes with you. Which we never did. I never did get around to it. But I never did take any of these jobs. I don't, I don't, there was no job that was worth it to me to, to take it away from anybody. That's when I started making these cards with, with, like, with Henry. I used to give out when, it's, like, Sidney Castane would say, Godfrey, give me one of your cards. I want to get in touch with you. I want to, I want to know how to get your band or something like that. I don't know if there was any here in there. No. It's not here. I think it's somewhere else. But I used to take a blank card on both sides and say, here's my card. I move around so much I don't even have time to put an address on the thing. And that was it. And, uh, that was it until, after a while, I mean, uh, Renee regarded me as a friend and knew that I wasn't out to chisel against him. Now, in fact, I worked with Renee before I gave up playing, I was supposed to work the whole carnival season with him. And then I had trouble with my eye. And I couldn't drive down to the, uh, auditorium. And then, uh, I was having a lot of trouble with my eye. So I just canceled the jobs. And I, uh, and a couple other jobs, you probably were on with me, with Cindy Castane, with things like that. And Renee had a great, like, one job that I played with him out at the Museum of, uh, New Orleans Museum of Arts. Uh, I came out the scene one night after, I think after, after we played Across the Lake. You remember when we played that New Year's Eve? Came over to see, uh, uh, uh, uh, we drove over there after the job. He says, what are you doing next Saturday night? I got a big wedding. I says, I'm doing nothing. He says, you got a job. He says, come on over. He said, be at the Museum of Art. He says, get there for such and such a time. I said, you don't have to hire me. He says, I want you. And then he was that kind of a guy. Uh-huh. You worked with Renee, didn't you? Sure, sure.
Sure.
He never, he was never cheap about anything.
No, that's right.
I can say one thing about Renee. Class act. He was, he was, he was okay. He was funny. He was a funny guy, but you had to know him to understand him. Sure.
He enjoyed being funny. He knew, he knew he was being that way and he, he enjoyed it.
Renee was something. So what else you want to know about me?
I want to know more about Ellis. Ellis Stratikas? We just touched on that. All right.

Ellis Stratikas, his father had a candy cigar and a candy store on one of the main streets in Gulfport, Mississippi. He was actually from Gulfport, Mississippi. That was his home. That was his, where he lived. Of course, he did, he married a woman and I remember her name. Her name was Sadie. See, the only thing I knew was Sadie Stratikas. She was a very gorgeous looking woman. Ellis was a very handsome guy. And they had a wonderful life together. And I don't know if Sadie's still alive, but... She passed away a year ago, I guess. Is that right? But Ellis, Ellis was a gentleman. If ever there was a gentleman. There was, well then, it's when, in later years, when, do you remember Slim Lamar?
I know the name, I never met him. I never met him.

He used to be a salesman for the Con Company when they were down on, on Coronelette Street, right off the canal across the street from the Music Box. Remember the Music Box where it was? Again, another name. Upstairs, upstairs.
I never got here until 45.

That's where we got our education in piano playing. Really? And faking. There was three piano players down there. Piano player never stopped. So they had to hire extra piano players. Okay. And there was Frank Bonero. I got that name on the tip of my tongue. He was, he was sort of a Spanish, he was a great arranger for Spanish music.
Was he, uh, Noem was well enough. Did he play with Johnny Wiggs, Johnny Honigman? No, uh-uh.
No.
He left town?
Yeah, he went to New York. He became, well, he became, he later became the second piano for the famous piano player, the orchestra leader. Oh, shit. Better than Horace Diaz? That's, that's his name.
That's his name.
How did you get that? Well, you described him. Well, you did a good job of describing it. He was an arranger, he was an arranger. Horace Diaz.
It was Horace Diaz, Frank Bonero, and myself. Well, Johnny Honigman used to talk about him. He really admired him.

He, uh, was he, I got the, I was with Horace and he was a good friend of Franzella's up in New York. And we used to go fishing. Mm-hmm. He sounded like I'd rather go fishing than eat. And we'd go out there and fish and we'd go fishing and spend the days together. And Horace was, uh, he was, in New York he was like, uh, Eddie, he was the second piano for Eddie Duchin. He played piano with Eddie Duchin's orchestra. And, uh, he is also an arranger for a southern music company. He made a lot of Horace Diaz. They had a lot of, a lot of Latin tunes when Latin first came out. He did a lot of Latin arrangements for southern music. Because I, I knew that, the, the professional manager up there. You see, I was in a position up there to know every professional manager in the business. Because I was him as manager. And we did all the broadcasting. Oh, really?
Yeah.

And I'd set up all the broadcasting acts with him as assistants. And, uh, in fact, I used to speak to Glenn Miller on an average of two to three times a week. Finding out, you see, in those days in, in radio, network radio, they were paid a royalty fee for the compositions. And, uh, the publisher, and the publisher, and the composer was, was getting a royalty. And, uh, that was on, on, on, on, on remotes. Remotes over, remotes over, uh, uh, networks. In other words, it was CBS, NBC, and ABC. It was, actually not, they're not, it wasn't ABC as yet, it was W.O.R. W.O.R. was, was ABC. And, uh, I'd ring up Glenn, and what are you gonna do this week? You know, well, you wanna do Sunday in New York, or you wanna do, blah, blah, blah, or, it isn't fair? And, that was Hymnless Compositions. Monday in New York, and It Isn't Fair, and a couple of other things that he wrote. And, uh, yeah. Well, I said, well, what do you want me to do? He said, well, do a serenade, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, you know, the sunrise serenade, or some shit like that. I can't remember the name of the title of it. And we talked every week, and that's, this is the way that these publishers, in fact, Hymnlessed me one time, that if I ever do a tune on the air for a kickback, he says, I'll fire you right now. He wouldn't allow me to take a dime or a dinner, or a lunch from even any one of these guys. And I didn't. There was one guy that, he was ready to commit suicide. I told him, I said, go ahead and kill yourself, I can't do a fucking thing for you.
Richard Hymnlessed was in several businesses. This is the guy you're talking about.

He was a producer. He was a, he had a brain that was so fast that people hated him. He, he, there was a girl by the name of, I can't remember her first name, but he finally changed her to by the name of Georgia Gibbs. Really? He changed her name to Georgia Gibbs. It was, I can't remember her.
It was an awful name if I remember.

She had another name and she used to record under that name when she wasn't with such and such a band, a band that she was with. And she was with us and, and Himba had an, Himba had the knack of, of giving people names. Same as Stuart Allen, who was our lead singer. Stuart Allen, his name was Allen Ross. Jewish boy. And we were doing Studebaker. And there was a, there was a fellow by the name of Joey Nash, who was a very fine singer. Was with the Himba band. And when he got the, when he got the, when he got the Studebaker show, the, the agency didn't want Joey Nash. Because Nash was the big advertising against Studebaker. Of course. If you want to mention the name Nash. So I'd ask him to change his name. Stuart Baker. He said, the hell with you, my name is Joey Nash and that's the way it's going to stay. And then they fired him. Then they got, Stuart Allen, so his name was Allen Ross, so he changed his name to, they wanted him to say Studebaker.
Did you tell him about being in here at P. Long's band?
No, no. That's interesting. No, I wasn't talking about that.
About the Colgate hour? I'm going down to Harrison, the other, to the shoe shop guy. I see y'all got this all the way down.
Let me.

So he, uh, so he got Stuart Allen. Stuart's dead too. He's dead, and Himba was dead for three days before. But you asked me about Himba if he had any other. He was in the, he was in the manufacturing business of magic tricks. I was talking to somebody the other day that knew that he had some of Himba's tricks. He had rings, finger rings, that were the most amazing thing in the world. They all come apart and you couldn't get them apart and you couldn't put them back together. Except if you move down. And it's the same thing with these rings that you, you have to put like this and put them apart and put them together. Yeah. But he was, he was in that. He was the one that invented the milk trick. Taking the milk and making a cornucopia of paper and pouring the milk into the, into the paper cornucopia and nothing goes in. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
